edges.description: Iron-associated metabolic stress and microstructural neuronal injury contribute to altered neural activity across sensorimotor and basal ganglia nodes of the dystonic network.
Aberrant somatosensory cortical and thalamic processing directly perturbs coupled cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical motor loop activity during speech preparation and execution.
Destabilized feedforward and feedback sensorimotor control of phonation triggers task-specific involuntary laryngeal motor drive during speech.
Reduced G-alpha-olf coupling of striatal D1 and A2A receptors is proposed to perturb basal ganglia dopaminergic signaling and, downstream, cortical preparatory and sensorimotor integrative activity.
Reduced motor cortical inhibition permits excessive corticobulbar drive to laryngeal motor neurons during speech.
Disinhibited motocortical and corticobulbar output drives excessive activation of brainstem phonatory lower motor neurons during speech.
Shared cortico-cerebellar-thalamic-basal ganglia network hyperfunction generates co-occurring agonist-antagonist dystonic vocal tremor in a substantial subset of patients.
Involuntary hyperactive motor discharges to intrinsic laryngeal muscles produce task-specific focal laryngeal dystonia during speech.
Spasmodic hyperadduction or untimely abduction of the vocal folds disrupts phonation and voice quality.
Hyperactive firing onto the thyroarytenoid and lateral cricoarytenoid muscles causes vocal fold hyperadduction with strained-strangled voice breaks in adductor disease.
Hyperactive firing onto the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle causes untimely vocal fold abduction with breathy, aphonic voice breaks in abductor disease.

Peripheral sensory-altering exposures (recurrent upper respiratory infection, gastroesophageal reflux, neck trauma) interact with central regions mediating sensorimotor preparation and integration in susceptible individuals.

nodes.description: Ultra-high-field (7 Tesla) quantitative susceptibility mapping with postmortem immunohistochemistry shows abnormal iron accumulation in sensorimotor and premotor cortices and subcortical nodes of the dystonic network. Iron-induced metabolic processes are proposed to drive microstructural neuronal damage that alters neural activity within the network, a recently described mechanistic layer of the disorder.

nodes.description: Targeted injection of botulinum toxin type A into the affected intrinsic laryngeal muscles (thyroarytenoid for adductor type; posterior cricoarytenoid for abductor type) is the first-line symptomatic treatment. It weakens the overactive muscles by cleaving SNAP-25 and blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, reducing spasms for several months per treatment cycle.

nodes.description: Spasmodic dysphonia is a central network disorder of the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical motor loop controlling laryngeal motor output. Functional and structural imaging implicate altered activity and connectivity across sensorimotor cortex, basal ganglia, thalamus, and cerebellum, with reduced striatal dopamine D2/D3 receptor binding, permitting excessive, involuntary laryngeal muscle activation during speech.

nodes.description: A heterozygous germline GNAL (DYT25) variant is found in a small minority of patients with isolated laryngeal dystonia (1 of 57 in the one screened cohort), with reduced penetrance. GNAL encodes G-alpha-olf, the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit that couples striatal dopamine D1 and adenosine A2A receptors to adenylyl cyclase. This node applies only to the GNAL-positive minority, not to spasmodic dysphonia generally.

evidence.reference_title: GNAL mutation in isolated laryngeal dystonia.

evidence.reference_title: GNAL mutation in isolated laryngeal dystonia.
evidence.snippet: GNAL encodes the stimulatory α subunit of the G protein, Golf, and has been linked to the mediation of odorant signaling in the olfactory epithelium 25, striatal dopaminergic signaling via coupling with D1 receptors of the direct pathway, and adenosine A2A receptors of the indirect pathway 26-31, as well as being co-localized with corticotropin-releasing hormone receptors in the cerebellar Purkinje cells 16.

nodes.description: Abnormal central processing of laryngeal sensory feedback contributes to the task-specific, action-induced nature of the dystonia. The primary somatosensory cortex and thalamic sensorimotor territories show consistent functional abnormalities, and deficient sensorimotor integration destabilizes feedforward/feedback control of phonation so that spasms appear selectively during the learned motor act of speech.

evidence.snippet: The primary somatosensory cortex shows consistent abnormalities in activation extent, intensity, correlation with other brain regions, and symptom severity in SD patients and, therefore, may be involved in the pathophysiology of SD.

nodes.description: The final common pathway is excessive, involuntary firing of laryngeal lower motor neurons (via the recurrent laryngeal nerve) onto intrinsic laryngeal muscles, producing the involuntary adductor or abductor spasms. Cholinergic neuromuscular transmission at the laryngeal muscle endplate is the site where botulinum toxin chemodenervation, the mainstay symptomatic therapy, acts; it is not itself abnormal in the disorder, so no neuromuscular signaling process is bound on this node.
